content: 1. Bisoprolol and hydrochlorothiazide are medications used in combination as a beta-adrenergic blocker and diuretic, respectively, and are FDA-approved for the treatment of hypertension. 2. Common side effects of this combination therapy include diarrhea, dizziness, headache, and fatigue. 3. For adults with hypertension, therapy is guided by clinical effect.5 mg to 20 mg of bisoprolol daily may be transitioned to the combination of bisoprolol fumarate and hydrochlorothiazide. 4. 5. Initial therapy typically begins with the lowest dose of bisoprolol fumarate and hydrochlorothiazide, such as 2.5 mg/6.25 mg taken orally once daily. 6. Subsequent dose titration may occur at 14-day intervals, with a maximum recommended dose of 20 mg/12.5 mg daily. 7. The combination therapy may replace the titrated individual components for convenience. 8. If discontinuation of bisoprolol fumarate and hydrochlorothiazide therapy is planned, it should be done gradually over approximately two weeks, with careful patient monitoring. 9. Caution is advised when dosing or titrating patients with renal or hepatic impairment. Since hydrochlorothiazide is not dialyzable and bisoprolol is minimally dialyzable, drug replacement is not necessary during dialysis. 10. Dosage adjustments based on age are generally not required for geriatric patients unless significant renal or hepatic dysfunction is present. 11. There is no established safety or efficacy data for pediatric use of bisoprolol fumarate and hydrochlorothiazide. 12. Off-label use of this combination in adults or pediatric patients is limited and not well-supported by guidelines. 13. Bisoprolol fumarate and hydrochlorothiazide are contraindicated in patients with cardiogenic shock, overt cardiac failure, secondor third-degree AV block, marked sinus bradycardia, anuria, or hypersensitivity to either component or sulfonamide-derived drugs. 14. Beta-blockers, including bisoprolol, should generally be avoided in patients with overt congestive heart failure, though they may be cautiously used in some cases of compensated heart failure. 15. Abrupt cessation of beta-blocker therapy can exacerbate angina pectoris, precipitate myocardial infarction, or cause ventricular arrhythmias in patients with coronary artery disease. Therapy should be tapered over approximately one week under careful observation. 16. Beta-blockers may precipitate or worsen symptoms of arterial insufficiency in patients with peripheral vascular disease. Caution is advised in such cases. 17. Patients with bronchospastic pulmonary disease should generally not receive beta-blockers. However, due to its relative beta-1 selectivity, bisoprolol fumarate may be used cautiously in patients who cannot tolerate other antihypertensive treatments. 18. Chronic beta-blocker therapy should not be routinely withdrawn before major surgery, as it may impair the heart's ability to respond to reflex adrenergic stimuli during anesthesia and surgery. 19. Beta-blockers may mask symptoms of hypoglycemia, such as tachycardia, and should be used cautiously in diabetic patients receiving insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents. 20. Beta-adrenergic blockade may also mask clinical signs of hyperthyroidism, such as tachycardia, and abrupt withdrawal may precipitate thyroid storm. 21. Thiazides, including hydrochlorothiazide, may cause cumulative effects in patients with impaired renal function, potentially leading to azotemia. Bisoprolol fumarate and hydrochlorothiazide should be discontinued if progressive renal impairment becomes apparent. 22. Thiazides may alter fluid and electrolyte balance, potentially precipitating hepatic coma in patients with impaired hepatic function or progressive liver disease. 23. 24. Periodic monitoring of serum electrolytes is recommended during therapy, as thiazides can cause hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypochloremic alkalosis, and hypomagnesemia. 25. Thiazides may also increase urinary magnesium excretion, potentially leading to hypomagnesemia. 26. Thiazides can decrease calcium excretion, and prolonged therapy may result in hypercalcemia and parathyroid gland changes. 27. Hyperuricemia or acute gout may be precipitated in some patients receiving thiazide diuretics. 28. Bisoprolol fumarate and hydrochlorothiazide are generally well-tolerated, with most adverse effects being mild and transient. 29. Common adverse effects include dizziness, headache, fatigue, bradycardia, gastrointestinal disturbances, and musculoskeletal pain. 30. Rare adverse effects include bronchospasm, skin reactions, and laboratory abnormalities such as increased uric acid, triglycerides, and liver enzymes. 31. Bisoprolol fumarate and hydrochlorothiazide may interact with other antihypertensive agents, catecholamine-depleting drugs, and certain calcium channel blockers, necessitating caution and close monitoring. 32. Thiazides may interact with alcohol, barbiturates, narcotics, antidiabetic drugs, corticosteroids, lithium, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, among others. 33. Bisoprolol fumarate and hydrochlorothiazide are classified as Pregnancy Category C by the FDA. Animal studies have shown fetotoxicity and maternotoxicity at high doses, but no teratogenic effects were observed. 34. The combination therapy should be used during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
